# Introduction

With the rapid expansion of heat pump installations across Swiss households,
electricity demand is increasingly driven by heating and cooling needs rather
than fixed consumption habits. Unlike traditional resistive heating, heat pumps
draw substantial power in short, weather-dependent bursts. This creates load
profiles that are harder to predict and more sensitive to outdoor conditions
than the appliance-driven consumption patterns that grid operators have
historically managed.

For energy suppliers and grid operators, this shift has direct economic
consequences. Procurement decisions made a day or week in advance are based on
load forecasts. When a cold snap arrives earlier than expected or a warm spell
pushes temperatures above the heating threshold, actual demand diverges from the
submitted schedule. The resulting imbalances must be settled at spot or
balancing energy prices. These costs ultimately flow back to households and
erode the economic case for electrification if not properly managed.

Against this background, this analysis systematically evaluates smart meter data
from a portfolio of heat pump households in Switzerland, using the **HEAPO
dataset**, in order to identify the most important drivers of electricity
consumption and build a well-founded basis for demand modelling. The focus is
not only on explaining consumption variability across seasonal patterns,
building characteristics, and technology choices, but also on quantifying the
interaction between external factors such as outdoor temperature, heating degree
days, and building type.

The report is structured as follows. Section 2 presents exploratory data
analysis. Section 3 fits and interprets six models, namely a Linear Model,
GLM Poisson, GLM Binomial, Generalised Additive Model, Neural Network, and
Support Vector Machine. Section 4 compares model performance. Section 5
draws conclusions for energy suppliers and grid operators.


## Dataset

**Source:** HEAPO – Household Energy and Smart Meter Data (Zenodo, 2025).

The HEAPO dataset was collected as part of a Swiss research project monitoring
residential heat pump installations via smart meters. It covers `r nrow(heapo)`
household-days across `r length(unique(heapo$Household_ID))` households observed
between 2022 and 2024, paired with daily weather data from the corresponding
measurement region. Each observation represents one household on one calendar
day, with daily electricity consumption as the primary outcome alongside a
set of building, technology, and weather covariates.

## Variable Description

| Variable | Type | Description |
|:---|:---|:---|
| `log_kWh_total` | Continuous | Natural log of daily total electricity consumption (kWh). Response for LM and GAM. |
| `heating_degree_days` | Continuous | Daily heating demand below the 12°C Swiss SIA base temperature (°C·day). |
| `temp_avg` | Continuous | Daily average outdoor temperature (°C). |
| `living_area` | Continuous | Heated floor area of the household (m²). |
| `building_type` | Categorical (>2 levels) | Building type, either "appartment" or "house". |
| `heatpump_type` | Categorical (2 levels) | Heat pump technology: air-source or ground-source. |
| `n_residents` | Count | Number of permanent household members. |
| `is_weekend` | Binary | 1 if Saturday or Sunday, 0 otherwise. |
| `has_floor_heating` | Binary | 1 if floor heating system present, 0 otherwise. |
| `high_consumption` | Binary | 1 if daily kWh exceeds the household's own 75th percentile (top 25% of that household's days). Response for GLM Binomial. |

The raw HEAPO dataset spans 2018 to 2024 across 438 monitored households in the
canton of Zurich. The modelling subset was restricted to the period 2022-01-01
through 2024-02-29 and limited to households with at least 95% daily coverage to
exclude partially observed installations. It was then randomly sampled to a
maximum of 100,000 observations to comply with the course data size limit.

# Exploratory Data Analysis

Daily electricity consumption (`kWh_total`) is right-skewed on the raw scale and
approximately symmetric after log transformation. The log-transformed variable
`log_kWh_total` is used as the continuous response in all regression models. The
binary variable `high_consumption` is derived from it. A day is classified as
high consumption if daily `log_kWh_total` exceeds that household's own 75th
percentile, flagging the top 25% of consumption days for each individual
household.

## Seasonal Pattern

```{r eda-seasonal, fig.height=4, fig.align='center'}
heapo %>%
  mutate(Month = month(date, label = TRUE, abbr = TRUE)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Month, y = kWh_total)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = clr_primary, alpha = 0.7, outlier.size = 0.2) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma) +
  labs(
    title = "Daily Electricity Consumption by Month",
    x = NULL,
    y = "kWh per day"
  ) +
  report_theme
```

Consumption in winter months (December to February) is roughly three to five
times higher than in summer (June to August), driven almost entirely by heat
pump operation for space heating. The wide interquartile range in winter
reflects differences in building size, insulation quality, and heat pump
technology across households. This strong seasonal pattern motivates heating
degree days as the primary weather predictor in all models.

## Heating Degree Days vs. Consumption

**Heating Degree Days (HDD)** quantify daily heating demand as the temperature
shortfall below the 12°C Swiss SIA base temperature. A day averaging 2°C
contributes 10 HDD, days above 12°C contribute zero. HDD is a more direct proxy
for heat pump workload than raw outdoor temperature.

```{r eda-hdd, fig.height=4, fig.align='center'}
heapo %>%
  slice_sample(n = 15000) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = heating_degree_days, y = kWh_total)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.08, size = 0.5, color = clr_primary) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "loess",
    color = clr_secondary,
    se = FALSE,
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma) +
  labs(
    title = "Heating Degree Days vs. Daily Consumption",
    subtitle = "Random subsample of 15,000 observations",
    x = "Heating Degree Days (HDD)",
    y = "kWh per day"
  ) +
  report_theme
```

The relationship is positive and seams to be linear across the observed
HDD range, with consumption measured form 0 to 125 kWh per day at 0 heating degree days
, which hints to the base load of the building types. The loess smoother confirms that no sharp threshold or strong
curvature is present, which justifies treating HDD as a continuous predictor in
the Linear Model. A slight levelling off at very high HDD values is visible, and
the GAM will capture this through its flexible smooth terms.

## Consumption by Building Type

```{r eda-building, fig.height=3.5, fig.align='center'}
heapo %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = building_type, y = kWh_total, fill = building_type)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7, outlier.size = 0.2) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = clr_builds, guide = "none") +
  labs(
    title = "Daily Consumption by Building Type",
    x = NULL,
    y = "kWh per day"
  ) +
  report_theme
```

Houses consume substantially more electricity per day than apartments, with medians
differing by roughly a factor of two. This gap persists after controlling for
weather, as the modelling section will confirm. Building type therefore carries
real structural signal and is included as a predictor in all models.

Taken together, the three plots tell a consistent story. Electricity demand is
primarily a seasonal phenomenon. The portfolio shifts from a low-consumption
summer baseline driven by domestic appliances to a high-consumption winter
regime dominated by heat pump space heating. Within that seasonal pattern,
building type is the strongest structural separator, with houses drawing
roughly twice the daily energy of apartments at any given temperature. These
findings directly shape the modelling choices below. The response is
log-transformed to stabilise variance, heating degree days enter as the
primary continuous weather predictor, and building type is retained as a
categorical covariate in every model. For the client, the key implication is
that cold spells and the building stock composition of a supply portfolio are
the two dominant levers of aggregate demand, and any forecasting tool must
capture both to be useful.

# Modelling

<!-- Each model section must:
       1. Fit the model to an appropriate response variable
       2. Interpret the coefficients in plain language (not just report p-values)
       3. State which group member led that section (at least 3 of the 6 models need a named lead)
     Models are saved as .RDS files and reloaded to speed up compilation. -->

Six models are fitted to the HEAPO data, each targeting a response variable
suited to its statistical family. The Linear Model and Generalised Additive
Model are fitted to `log_kWh_total`, the log-transformed daily electricity
consumption. The GLM Binomial, Neural Network, and Support Vector Machine all classify
household-days as high or low consumption using each household's own 75th
percentile as the threshold, capturing the top 25% of days for each individual
household. The GLM Poisson
models the monthly count of high-consumption days per household, capturing
longer-term demand patterns at a coarser aggregation. Model performance is
evaluated in the comparison section: regression models are compared via
five-fold cross-validation MAE in kWh and R²; classification models via AUC
and accuracy.

## Linear Model (LM) {#lm}

*Lead: Tharrmeehan Krishnathasan*

```{r import-lm, echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
heapo_lm <- readRDS("../models/linear_model/heapo_lm.rds")

mlm_simple_path <- "../models/linear_model/heapo_mlm_simple.rds"
if (file.exists(mlm_simple_path)) {
  heapo_mlm_simple <- readRDS(mlm_simple_path)
} else {
  heapo_mlm_simple <- lm(
    log_kWh_total ~ heating_degree_days +
      sunshine_hours +
      humidity_avg +
      living_area +
      n_residents +
      building_type +
      heatpump_type,
    data = heapo
  )
  saveRDS(heapo_mlm_simple, mlm_simple_path)
}
```

### Objective

This section models daily household energy consumption as $\text{log\_kWh\_total}$, the natural logarithm of total daily kilowatt-hour usage. The log transformation is standard for energy data: daily kWh is strictly positive and right-skewed in raw form, and approximately normal on the log scale.

Predictors cover weather conditions (heating degree days, sunshine hours, humidity), building characteristics (building type, living area, heat pump type), and household composition (number of residents). Two interaction terms are added to test whether cold-weather sensitivity differs by building type and heat pump technology.

### Model Setup

Two models are estimated:

**Simple MLR:** all seven predictors with main effects only, as an interpretable baseline for the additive relationships between predictors and log energy consumption:

$$
\log(\text{kWh}_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{HDD}_i + \beta_2\,\text{Sunshine}_i + \cdots + \beta_7\,\text{HeatpumpType}_i + \varepsilon_i
$$

**Extended MLR:** adds two interaction terms motivated by domain knowledge:

- $\text{heating\_degree\_days} \times \text{heatpump\_type}$: different heat
  pump technologies have different efficiencies in cold conditions, so the
  effect of cold on consumption should vary by pump type.
- $\text{heating\_degree\_days} \times \text{building\_type}$: houses and
  apartments differ structurally in size, exposed surface area, and construction,
  so their cold-weather sensitivity is expected to differ.

All coefficients are on the log scale: a coefficient of 0.05 means a 5%
multiplicative change in kWh for a one-unit increase in the predictor.

The panel structure (multiple observations per household) means the i.i.d. assumption of standard OLS is not fully met; standard errors may be slightly understated due to within-household correlation.

### Model Results

<details>
<summary>Show / hide table</summary>
```{r lm-coef-table, echo=TRUE}
tidy(heapo_lm) %>%
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") %>%
  mutate(
    estimate = round(estimate, 4),
    std.error = round(std.error, 4),
    statistic = round(statistic, 2),
    p.value = signif(p.value, 3)
  ) %>%
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Predictor", "Estimate", "Std. Error", "t value", "p value"),
    caption = "Extended MLR: coefficient estimates"
  ) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"), full_width = TRUE)
```
</details>

All predictors are significant at the 0.001 level except `humidity_avg` (p = 0.165), which adds nothing once the other weather variables are included. Effects on log energy consumption, holding all other variables constant:

**Heating degree days** (β = 0.021, p < 0.001): Each additional HDD increases log consumption by ~2.1% for air-source pump households in apartments (the baseline group).

**Sunshine hours** (β = −0.015, p < 0.001): An additional sunshine hour reduces
consumption by ~1.5%, reflecting lower heating demand on brighter days.

**Number of residents** (β = 0.134, p < 0.001): Each additional resident
increases consumption by ~14.3% ($e^{0.134} - 1$), the second strongest effect
after the temperature-building interaction.

**Building type — house** (β = 0.220, p < 0.001): Houses consume ~24.6% more than apartments at baseline, before accounting for their greater sensitivity to cold (see interaction below).

**Heat pump type — ground-source** (β = −0.143, p < 0.001): Ground-source pump
households consume ~13.3% less than air-source households at the baseline
temperature.

**Interaction: HDD × house** (β = 0.039, p < 0.001): Houses are substantially *more* sensitive to cold than apartments: each additional HDD adds 3.9% to log consumption, the largest interaction effect in the model.

**Interaction: HDD × ground-source** (β = −0.003, p < 0.001): Ground-source pump
households are slightly *less* sensitive to cold than air-source households,
consistent with the higher efficiency of ground-source systems at low outdoor
temperatures.

### Visual Evidence

The coefficient plot below summarises the direction and significance of all predictors in the extended model.

```{r lm-coef-plot, echo=TRUE, fig.height=5, fig.width=8, out.width="100%", fig.align="center"}
cis <- confint(heapo_lm)

coef_df <- tibble(
  term = names(coef(heapo_lm)),
  estimate = coef(heapo_lm),
  lower = cis[, 1],
  upper = cis[, 2]
) %>%
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") %>%
  mutate(significant = !(lower < 0 & upper > 0))

ggplot(
  coef_df,
  aes(x = estimate, y = reorder(term, estimate), color = significant)
) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = lower, xmax = upper), height = 0.3) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = clr_neutral) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("FALSE" = clr_neutral, "TRUE" = clr_primary),
    labels = c("n.s.", "p < 0.05")
  ) +
  report_theme +
  labs(
    title = "Linear Model – Coefficient Estimates with 95% CIs",
    subtitle = "Coefficients on log scale — positive = higher consumption",
    x = "Coefficient estimate",
    y = NULL,
    color = NULL
  )
```

The scatterplot of observed versus fitted values on the log scale illustrates the model's predictive fit. Points near the diagonal indicate accurate predictions.

```{r lm-obs-vs-fit, echo=TRUE, fig.height=3.5, fig.width=5.5, out.width="70%", fig.align="center"}
fit_df <- tibble(
  fitted = fitted(heapo_lm),
  observed = heapo$log_kWh_total[as.integer(names(fitted(heapo_lm)))]
)

ggplot(fit_df, aes(x = fitted, y = observed)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.15, size = 0.8, color = clr_primary) +
  geom_abline(
    slope = 1,
    intercept = 0,
    color = clr_secondary,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  report_theme +
  labs(
    title = "Observed vs. Fitted (log kWh)",
    x = "Fitted values",
    y = "Observed values"
  )
```

### Model Diagnostics

p2 <- ggplot(aug, aes(sample = .std.resid)) +

    y = expression(sqrt("|Std. residuals|"))

p4 <- ggplot(aug, aes(x = .hat, y = .std.resid)) +

    method = "loess",

  ) +
