### Model Diagnostics

Unlike regression models, SVM diagnostics focus on generalisation performance and modelling choices rather than distributional assumptions.

**CV tuning results:** Across all 9 combinations, CV accuracy ranged from 0.8071 (C=10, sigma=0.01) to 0.8304 (C=100, sigma=0.1429). The top four combinations all involve sigma ≥ 0.1, suggesting a moderately local kernel works best. The gain from increasing C from 10 to 100 at sigma=0.1429 is small (0.8268 → 0.8304), with diminishing returns beyond that.

**Class separability:** The available predictors do not reliably separate the two classes. High and normal consumption days share substantial overlap in the feature space, which no kernel choice can resolve.

**Tuning stability:** The best combination (C=`r best_C`, sigma=`r best_sigma`) sits at the top-right corner of the grid. The gain from C=10 to C=100 at sigma=0.1429 is small (0.8268 → 0.8304), pointing to the predictor set as the limiting factor rather than model configuration.

### Key Findings

**The SVM achieves reasonable accuracy but low sensitivity:** At `r round(cm_best$overall["Accuracy"] * 100, 1)`% accuracy, the model scores roughly 8 percentage points above the naive majority-class baseline (`r round(table(test_y)["normal"] / length(test_y) * 100, 1)`%). Sensitivity of `r round(cm_best$byClass["Sensitivity"] * 100, 1)`% is the bigger concern: more than half of actual high-consumption days are missed, while specificity of `r round(cm_best$byClass["Specificity"] * 100, 1)`% shows the model rarely raises false alarms on normal days. This makes it too conservative on its own for capacity planning or demand-response triggering.

**Tuning yields real but limited improvement:** Moving from default parameters to C=`r best_C`, sigma=`r best_sigma` improves sensitivity from `r round(cm_baseline$byClass["Sensitivity"] * 100, 1)`% to `r round(cm_best$byClass["Sensitivity"] * 100, 1)`% and accuracy from `r round(cm_baseline$overall["Accuracy"] * 100, 1)`% to `r round(cm_best$overall["Accuracy"] * 100, 1)`%. The gains are consistent but small; further tuning will not resolve the core problem.

**The predictor set is the bottleneck:** Weather conditions and static household characteristics capture only part of what drives high-consumption days. High and normal consumption days overlap substantially in the feature space, and no kernel or regularisation choice can separate what is genuinely mixed in the data. Richer features would help: lagged consumption, occupancy patterns, or appliance-level data.

**Threshold adjustment is a practical alternative:** Lowering the flagging threshold would recover more true positives at the cost of more false alarms, which may be acceptable in a probabilistic forecasting pipeline. At the default threshold, the model should not be the sole basis for high-consumption day decisions.

# Model Comparison {#comparison}

The six models do not all share the same response variable, so a single
unified comparison table is not possible. Instead, models are grouped by
what they predict. Regression models (LM and GAM) are evaluated on
`log_kWh_total` using five-fold cross-validation mean absolute error in kWh
and R². Classification models (GLM Binomial, Neural Network, SVM) are
evaluated on `high_consumption` using five-fold CV AUC and accuracy. The
GLM Poisson targets a monthly count at a different aggregation level and is
assessed separately. In all cases, the same random fold assignment is used
across models within each group so that fold-to-fold variation cancels out
and differences reflect only model quality.

## Regression Models: LM vs GAM

```{r reg-comparison-load, echo=FALSE}
if (file.exists("../models/cv_reg_results.rds")) {
  reg_summary <- readRDS("../models/cv_reg_results.rds")
} else {
  reg_summary <- NULL
}
```

The table below reports five-fold cross-validation performance for the two
regression models fitted to `log_kWh_total`. MAE is computed on the original
kWh scale for interpretability. R² is computed on the log scale.

```{r reg-comparison-table, echo=FALSE}
if (!is.null(reg_summary)) {
  knitr::kable(
    reg_summary,
    caption = paste(
      "Five-fold CV performance: regression models on log_kWh_total.",
      "MAE is on the kWh scale; R² is on the log scale."
    )
  ) %>%
    kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"), full_width = TRUE)
} else {
  cat("*Table not available. Run R/04_model_comparison_cv.R first.*")
}
```

```{r reg-comparison-plot, echo=FALSE, fig.height=3.5, fig.align='center'}
if (!is.null(reg_summary)) {
  reg_long <- tidyr::pivot_longer(
    reg_summary,
    cols = -Model,
    names_to = "Metric",
    values_to = "Value"
  )

  print(
    ggplot(reg_long, aes(x = Model, y = Value, fill = Model)) +
      geom_col(width = 0.5, show.legend = FALSE) +
      scale_fill_manual(values = c(clr_primary, clr_secondary)) +
      facet_wrap(~Metric, scales = "free_y") +
      report_theme +
      labs(
        title = "5-fold CV: LM vs GAM",
        x = NULL,
        y = NULL
      )
  )
}
```

Both models use **exactly the same predictor set**: heating degree days
(interacted with building type and heat pump type), sunshine hours, humidity,
living area, and number of residents. The only difference is functional form:
the LM uses linear terms and explicit interaction dummies, while the GAM
replaces these with `by =` smooths. This makes the comparison controlled and
directly attributable to model flexibility rather than predictor choice.

The GAM achieves a CV MAE of
`r reg_summary[grepl("GAM", reg_summary$Model), "CV MAE (kWh/day)"]` kWh/day
and an R² of `r reg_summary[grepl("GAM", reg_summary$Model), "CV R2"]`,
compared to
`r reg_summary[grepl("Linear", reg_summary$Model), "CV MAE (kWh/day)"]` kWh/day
and R² of `r reg_summary[grepl("Linear", reg_summary$Model), "CV R2"]` for the
extended LM. The GAM reduces prediction error by
`r round(reg_summary[grepl("Linear", reg_summary$Model), "CV MAE (kWh/day)"] - reg_summary[grepl("GAM", reg_summary$Model), "CV MAE (kWh/day)"], 2)`
kWh/day, a roughly 3.6% improvement, and explains 3.6 additional percentage
points of variance. The improvement is real but modest. As the GAM smooth plots
showed, the main non-linearity is in how houses respond to extreme cold (edf =
5.3 for s(HDD):house), but this effect does not translate into a large
out-of-sample accuracy gain. This suggests that household-level heterogeneity,
not functional form, is the primary source of unexplained variance.

For a client who prioritises interpretability, the extended LM is a reasonable
choice: its coefficients are directly actionable and its predictions are nearly
as accurate. For a client who prioritises predictive performance, the GAM is
preferred, but the marginal gain of 0.40 kWh/day should be weighed against the
added complexity of smooth terms and the loss of a single interpretable
coefficient per predictor.

## Classification Models: GLM Binomial vs SVM vs Neural Network

```{r class-comparison-load, echo=FALSE}
if (file.exists("../models/cv_class_results.rds")) {
  class_summary <- readRDS("../models/cv_class_results.rds")
} else {
  class_summary <- NULL
}
```

The table below compares all three classification models. All three use each 
household's own 75th percentile as the high-consumption threshold, making 
results directly comparable. CV results are available for all three models.

```{r class-comparison-table, echo=FALSE}
if (!is.null(class_summary)) {
  knitr::kable(
    class_summary,
    caption = paste(
      "Classification model performance.",
      "All models: 5-fold CV, per-household 75th percentile threshold."
    )
  ) %>%
    kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"), full_width = TRUE)
} else {
  cat(
    "*CV table not available. Run R/04_model_comparison_cv_classification.R then R/3.5_neural_network.R first.*"
  )
}
```

```{r class-comparison-plot, echo=FALSE, fig.height=3.5, fig.align='center'}
if (!is.null(class_summary)) {
  plot_data <- tidyr::pivot_longer(
    class_summary,
    cols = -Model,
    names_to = "Metric",
    values_to = "Value"
  )
  print(
    ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = Model, y = Value, fill = Model)) +
      geom_col(width = 0.5, show.legend = FALSE) +
      scale_fill_manual(values = c(clr_primary, clr_neutral, clr_secondary)) +
      facet_wrap(~Metric, scales = "free_y") +
      report_theme +
      labs(
        title = "Classification model comparison",
        subtitle = "All models: per-household 75th percentile threshold",
        x = NULL,
        y = NULL
      )
  )
}
```

All three models share the same per-household 75th percentile threshold, making them directly comparable. The GLM
Binomial achieves a higher AUC (`r round(class_summary[grepl("GLM", class_summary$Model), "CV AUC"], 3)` vs `r round(class_summary[grepl("SVM", class_summary$Model), "CV AUC"], 3)`) while accuracy is essentially tied (`r round(class_summary[grepl("GLM", class_summary$Model), "CV Accuracy"] * 100, 1)`% vs `r round(class_summary[grepl("SVM", class_summary$Model), "CV Accuracy"] * 100, 1)`%). The AUC gap reflects the GLM's stronger overall discrimination across all classification thresholds. Both models correctly identify roughly four out of five household-days. The GLM Binomial is the preferred choice: it matches the SVM on accuracy, outperforms it on AUC, and provides explicit odds ratios for each predictor. For a client who needs to explain predictions (for example, when flagging a household for an energy audit), this interpretability advantage is directly actionable.

## GLM Poisson (Standalone)

The GLM Poisson models `n_high_days` at the household–month level and
cannot be placed in either comparison table. It is evaluated separately
via five-fold CV RMSE on the count scale.

```{r poisson-cv, echo=TRUE, cache=TRUE}
set.seed(42)

# Extract formula cleanly — detach from model environment to avoid memory bleed
cv_form <- as.formula(
  deparse(formula(mod_pois)),
  env = baseenv()
)

n <- nrow(dat_count)
folds <- sample(rep(1:5, length.out = n))
rmse_folds <- numeric(5)

for (k in 1:5) {
  train_k <- dat_count[folds != k, ]
  test_k <- dat_count[folds == k, ]

  fit_k <- glm(
    cv_form,
    family = poisson(link = "log"),
    offset = log(n_days),
    data = train_k,
    model = FALSE,
    x = FALSE,
    y = FALSE
  )

  pred_k <- predict(fit_k, newdata = test_k, type = "response")
  rmse_folds[k] <- sqrt(mean((test_k$n_high_days - pred_k)^2))
  rm(fit_k, train_k, test_k)
  gc()
}

pois_cv_rmse <- round(mean(rmse_folds), 3)
pois_cv_sd <- round(sd(rmse_folds), 3)
```

The five-fold CV RMSE is `r pois_cv_rmse` days (SD = `r pois_cv_sd`).
Given that `n_high_days` ranges from 0 to ~30, this reflects moderate
prediction error on the count scale.

**Limitation.** This RMSE is not directly comparable to any other metric
in this report: the unit of observation is a household–month and the
response is a raw count. Cross-model ranking would be misleading.

Across all six models, interpretability and predictive performance trade
off consistently. The LM, GAMs, and GLM Poisson offer transparent,
coefficient-based explanations but leave more variance unexplained. The
SVM and Neural Network improve accuracy but are effectively black boxes.
The GLM Binomial sits in between — log-odds coefficients remain
interpretable while classification performance is competitive. The right
choice depends on whether the use case demands explainability or accuracy.

# Conclusions {#conclusions}

Across 127 Swiss households monitored daily from 2022 to 2024, this analysis
identified the key drivers of heat pump electricity consumption and built a
foundation for demand modelling relevant to grid operators and energy suppliers.

Cold weather is the strongest structural driver of daily consumption, but its
effect is not uniform. Houses show a sharply accelerating response on the
coldest winter days, a pattern that has direct implications for load forecasting
during cold snaps and that a plain linear model understates. Beyond weather,
heat pump type and occupancy are the two most consistent predictors across all
models. Ground-source heat pumps consume approximately 13% less electricity per
day than air-source systems, and every additional resident adds roughly 14% to
daily demand regardless of building type or season.

For classifying unusually high-demand days, weekend occupancy is the single
strongest predictor, with cold weather second. Structural characteristics become
non-significant once the model accounts for each household's own baseline,
meaning demand spikes are driven by behaviour and weather rather than building
or system properties.

The GAM achieved the best predictive accuracy for daily consumption with a MAE
of 10.6 kWh per day and an R² of 31%, modestly improving on the Linear Model.
Both models leave roughly two thirds of day-to-day variation unexplained,
pointing to the value of incorporating behavioural signals in future work. For
classification, the Neural Network achieved the strongest performance with an
AUC of `r round(class_summary[grepl("Neural", class_summary$Model), "CV AUC"], 3)`
and accuracy of `r round(class_summary[grepl("Neural", class_summary$Model), "CV Accuracy"] * 100, 1)`%,
with the SVM close behind at an AUC of
`r round(class_summary[grepl("SVM", class_summary$Model), "CV AUC"], 3)`
and accuracy of
`r round(class_summary[grepl("SVM", class_summary$Model), "CV Accuracy"] * 100, 1)`%.
For a client prioritising transparency, the GLM Binomial is recommended,
achieving an AUC of
`r round(class_summary[grepl("GLM", class_summary$Model), "CV AUC"], 3)`
and accuracy of
`r round(class_summary[grepl("GLM", class_summary$Model), "CV Accuracy"] * 100, 1)`%
while remaining fully interpretable.

The practical implication for energy suppliers and grid operators is to target
demand management programmes at larger households with air-source systems during
cold weather peaks, where high occupancy and less efficient heating combine to
produce the sharpest load spikes. Weekend time-of-use tariffs or demand response
incentives offer an additional lever for flattening the load peaks that drive
balancing energy costs.

# Use of Generative AI {#ai}

Generative AI tools — primarily Claude (Anthropic) and GitHub Copilot — were used throughout this project to support code generation, debugging, and text drafting. AI assistance proved effective for producing boilerplate R code for data preprocessing, visualisation, and model-fitting wrappers, as well as for generating first drafts of methodological prose describing model outputs and statistical concepts. Human oversight was essential for tasks requiring analytical judgement, including the selection of modelling thresholds, cross-validation architecture, and the interpretation of model coefficients, where AI-generated suggestions occasionally contained subtle errors or overstated certainty. All AI-generated code was reviewed and tested prior to integration, and all interpretive text was verified against actual model output before inclusion in this report.
